Cancer’s Radioisotope Bottleneck Has Moved Downstream

Cancer drug analysis usually starts with the molecule: the target, the response rate, the safety profile and the size of the eligible population. Radiopharmaceuticals add an industrial question. Can the developer convert a radioactive isotope into a regulatorily usable dose, release it on time, move it through licensed transport and place it in front of a prepared patient before decay consumes its value?

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-06-23 · 13 min read

In brief

  • $2.810B | 2025 Lu-177 product sales show commercial radioligand therapy already operates at scale.
  • 10 days | Ac-225 decay makes qualification, release and delivery part of the product.
  • 50–100 mCi | DOE’s current accelerator batch range remains small for broad commercial demand.
  • $450M | TerraPower is funding a large cGMP Ac-225 manufacturing buildout.
  • Two suppliers | repeatable procurement would move the bottleneck beyond qualified isotope.

The scarce object is no longer radioactivity alone

Facility / lab photo

TerraPower Isotopes scientists working on cancer treatments

Scientists in a radiochemistry environment show that radiopharma scale-up is a facility and process problem, not only a molecule problem.

Open source visual from TerraPower Isotopes

Reuse: license unclear - rights not verified · Attribution: TerraPower Isotopes

That question becomes more important after the biology begins to work. A successful radiopharmaceutical does not behave like a tablet that can sit in a warehouse. It behaves like a scheduled manufacturing event. Source material, irradiation, radiochemical separation, cGMP processing, ligand conjugation, fill-finish, quality control, transport and hospital administration must align around a physical clock.

The strongest version of the original scarcity thesis does not survive scrutiny. Commercial lutetium-177 supply has already reached scaled operation. The narrower thesis does: for actinium-225, the difficult object is still qualified, referenceable and deliverable isotope, not nominal radioactivity. The constraint is route-specific and sequential rather than uniform across radiopharma.

That distinction matters. TerraPower has reported weekly commercial-scale Ac-225 starting-material production since October 2024, but says the material requires further manufacturing and is not itself produced under cGMP. Raw supply can improve while purification, documentation, release and drug-product conversion remain scarce.

Lu-177 shows how a bottleneck can move

Pluvicto provides the most useful commercial case because its shortage both appeared and cleared. Novartis reported in October 2023 that FDA had classified the shortage as resolved after weekly production capacity more than doubled. At the time, more than 200 centers were actively ordering the therapy and about 130 more were planned. (Novartis Pluvicto supply update)

The recovery weakens the idea that isotope scarcity must become a permanent source of rent. Novartis added manufacturing capacity, gained site approvals and expanded the treatment network. Pluvicto then produced $1.994 billion of 2025 net sales, while Lutathera produced $816 million. The combined $2.810 billion confirms that radioligand therapy can move through the manufacturing and administration chain at commercial scale. (Novartis product sales)

It also shows where the bottleneck went. Indianapolis added a 70,000-square-foot FDA-approved site in 2024. The reported 250,000-dose figure applied to Novartis’s then four-site RLT network, not Indianapolis alone. Carlsbad added a 10,000-square-foot western U.S. site in 2025. Denton, Texas, is a 46,000-square-foot project expected to operate in 2028, while Winter Park, Florida, is scheduled for 2029. (Novartis Indianapolis approval)

The operating logic is geographic. When treatment depends on a short-lived dose and a fixed patient appointment, the manufacturer cannot rely on ordinary inventory buffers. Regional production protects release windows, transport time and treatment-day reliability.

Lu-177 therefore does not disprove the isotope-clock mechanism. It demonstrates its sequential character. Once upstream supply and manufacturing improve, the constraint can migrate into regional release capacity, companion imaging, nuclear-medicine staffing, radiation-safety procedures and patient scheduling.

Ac-225 is still a qualification problem

Actinium-225 remains less mature. DOE describes it as a high-demand isotope with limited availability. Its accelerator route has distributed more than 1,102 millicuries, with current batches around 50–100 millicuries. DOE also describes a planned move toward batches of 100–1,000 millicuries, although the source does not provide a reliable calendar origin for its stated four-year horizon. (DOE Ac-225 overview)

The physical bottleneck is visible inside that production route. Brookhaven said available hot-cell space had limited Ac-225 processing. An $8.5 million refurbishment returned dormant hot cells to service, doubled DOE processing sites and enabled Brookhaven to process irradiated thorium targets and ship material to customers. (DOE Brookhaven hot cells)

Oak Ridge controls another layer. FDA acknowledged ORNL’s drug master file for Ac-225 nitrate, allowing sponsors with authorization to reference confidential manufacturing information in their submissions. A DMF is not an approval of the isotope or of a finished drug. Its commercial importance is that it can reduce repeated regulatory work and embed a particular production route in sponsor filings. (ORNL Ac-225 DMF)

Private conversion capacity is also moving beyond the planning stage. Cardinal Health said in April 2026 that it had quadrupled weekly Ac-225 output since routine production began in late 2024, added a high-capacity line to its DMF and supplied material supporting more than 15 clinical trials. (Cardinal Health Ac-225 expansion)

Bristol Myers Squibb offers a second operating case. By July 2025, its 77,000-square-foot RayzeBio hub in Indianapolis was fully operational for clinical orders, producing human clinical doses and offering delivery within three days after release. That does not establish abundant or interchangeable Ac-225 supply. It does show that an integrated sponsor can already move an alpha-radiopharmaceutical through the chain. (BMS RayzeBio hub)

The capacity race is real, but announcements are not output

The next wave of projects is large enough to change the market if commissioning, cGMP validation and customer qualification occur on schedule.

TerraPower says Bellwether could increase global Ac-225 capacity twentyfold. That remains a company target, not delivered output; the public record does not disclose a curies-per-year baseline that independently validates the multiple. (TerraPower Bellwether)

PanTera says its Belgian project has obtained nuclear and environmental permits and targets first commercial supply in 2029. The underlying permit files were not independently examined in the report, so the timing should remain attributed to the project issuer. (PanTera project)

Nusano illustrates why floor space and ribbon cuttings are weak proxies. Its 190,000-square-foot Utah facility was previously associated with late-2025 production expectations. A June 2026 update instead placed the platform at the first of three commissioning milestones, with a production-capability demonstration scheduled for September and full-platform validation targeted for December 2026. (Nusano commissioning)

The industrial lesson is simple: a building is not a batch, a batch is not a released lot, and a released lot is not repeatable procurement.

Control may move without margin moving

The radiopharmaceutical value chain contains several possible control points. Isotope producers control source materials, irradiation routes and radionuclidic purity. DMF holders control referenceable manufacturing information. CDMOs control development slots, technical transfer, aseptic processing and release. Nuclear-pharmacy networks control preparation and regional delivery. Hospitals control licensed personnel, radiation-safety workflows and the patient calendar.

Capital is already moving into these layers. TerraPower has committed $450 million to Bellwether. Nucleus RadioPharma raised $50 million for expansion in Rochester and a planned Philadelphia facility. Novartis is building a regional manufacturing network, while BMS internalized manufacturing through the RayzeBio acquisition and Indianapolis hub.

But capital migration is not the same as margin migration.

Public supply agreements generally do not disclose isotope price, committed volume, priority rights, minimum purchases, utilization, gross margin or remedies for non-delivery. The Nucleus–BWXT framework covers GMP-grade Ac-225 and I-123 and requires BWXT to maintain product DMFs and provide letters of authorization. That verifies a procurement and regulatory structure, but not supplier economics. (Nucleus–BWXT agreement)

Vertical integration may allow drug sponsors to retain most value. Novartis can use its manufacturing network to protect product revenue and launch execution without creating a separately visible supplier profit pool. BMS can absorb manufacturing, quality and logistics economics inside a broader drug franchise. Cardinal Health can bundle isotope conversion with its national nuclear-pharmacy footprint rather than expose Ac-225 as a standalone segment.

Independent CDMOs may still benefit, particularly when smaller sponsors cannot justify their own hot cells, licenses, analytical systems and logistics network. Nucleus has paired manufacturing with regulatory support, isotope procurement and shipment capabilities. Its alliances and commercial agreements show demand for that bundle. The unresolved question is whether the bundle earns differentiated margins or mainly passes through expensive isotope and courier costs.

Hospitals face the same ambiguity. Medicare provides payment mechanisms for separately payable therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals, but the report does not establish whether reimbursement fully covers authorized-user staffing, imaging, shielding, radiation safety and scheduling. A functioning payment rail is necessary for adoption; it is not proof of attractive provider economics.

The historical base rate cuts both ways

The closest broad precedent is the Mo-99/Tc-99m shortage of 2009–2010. Outages at a small number of research reactors produced a global supply shock, and the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency later emphasized economic sustainability and outage-reserve capacity. The IAEA reported a 30% shortfall during the 2008–2009 outage period, with diagnostic procedures postponed. (IAEA isotope shortage)

The similarity is concentrated infrastructure serving time-sensitive medical demand. A small number of failures can interrupt care because radioactive products cannot be stockpiled like ordinary pharmaceuticals.

The difference is the therapeutic chain. Ac-225 and Lu-177 require cGMP isotope API, drug conjugation, product-specific release, oncology scheduling and licensed administration. A reactor or accelerator can be operating while the clinically useful dose remains unavailable.

Pluvicto supplies a more direct therapeutic precedent. Its shortage was serious enough to constrain new patient starts, yet manufacturing expansion and regulatory approvals resolved it within the launch cycle. That episode argues against treating every shortage as structurally permanent. It also confirms that physical and regulatory infrastructure can pace a successful therapy until the sponsor adds enough capacity.

The base rate therefore supports fragility, not permanent scarcity. The relevant question is how long qualification and conversion remain concentrated before redundancy arrives.

The strongest counterargument is faster relief—or weaker demand

The first counterargument is that relief is already moving faster than the late-2020s thesis assumes. Cardinal is scaling qualified conversion. RayzeBio is producing clinical doses. DOE has added hot-cell redundancy. TerraPower is producing starting material. Nusano, Bellwether and PanTera could add new routes before broad alpha-therapy demand reaches the market.

If those routes qualify on schedule, Ac-225 procurement could become ordinary before scarcity meaningfully affects commercial launches. Under that scenario, the bottleneck moves into drug-product manufacturing, release laboratories, logistics, imaging and treatment centers.

The second counterargument is weaker demand. Most Ac-225 products remain investigational. Efficacy, durability and safety will determine whether planned facilities serve a large market or become underused assets. Early Novartis AcTION data were encouraging, but reported adverse events included dry mouth and severe anemia. Those findings require larger trials and should not be converted into a commercial-demand forecast. (Reuters on AcTION)

Supply pressure is also uneven. The report identifies Ac-225 trials suspended for drug-supply reasons, evidence that shortages can still interrupt individual programs. Yet other alpha programs have progressed through Phase 3 infrastructure. The market may contain local failures and successful workarounds at the same time.

The thesis is wrong if qualified material becomes interchangeable before demand scales. It is also wrong if alpha therapies fail to create enough demand for the new capacity. The middle case—successful drugs arriving before redundant procurement—remains the scenario in which the qualification gate matters most.

What to watch

  • September 30, 2026: Nusano completes or delays its full-LINAC beam-to-target demonstration.
  • December 31, 2026: Nusano validates its production platform or resets the commissioning schedule.
  • December 31, 2027: ACTION-1 records primary completion or moves its date beyond 2027.
  • December 31, 2028: two non-DOE suppliers establish four consecutive quarters of multi-sponsor qualified deliveries.
  • December 31, 2029: TerraPower releases Bellwether’s first cGMP Ac-225 lot or revises its target.
  • December 31, 2030: repeatable Ac-225 procurement becomes multi-supplier, or qualification remains non-redundant.

Radiopharma’s commercial constraint is no longer one thing. Lu-177 shows that manufacturing shortages can be solved. Ac-225 shows that raw production can expand before qualified, referenceable and deliverable supply becomes routine. The durable advantage, if one emerges, will belong to the actor that can repeatedly turn isotope into an accepted patient dose. The evidence does not yet show who will retain the margin from doing so.
